issues.description: is_registered mutation on shared TritonLoraConfig creates a race condition
issues.detail: TritonLoraConfig is held in TritonModelMetadata and shared across all concurrent requests. _create_trtllm_generate_request reads is_registered, then loads weights, then sets is_registered=True with no lock. Two concurrent first-time requests for the same LoRA will both see is_registered=False, both load the .npy files, both send full weights downstream, and the flag flips twice. Worse: a request that sees is_registered=True can race ahead of the request that's still loading and send only task_id to a backend that hasn't cached the weights yet. The data structure conflates immutable config (name, path, task_id) with mutable runtime state (is_registered) — split them, or guard the registration with a per-config lock.

issues.description: lora_config_path variable is shadowed inside the loop, corrupting the outer path
issues.detail: In _parse_lora_configs the outer scope binds lora_config_path = os.path.join(version_path, 'multi_lora.json'). Inside the per-entry loop the same name is rebound to os.path.join(lora_path, 'model.lora_config.npy'). On the next repo iteration the multi_lora.json path is gone, replaced by the last per-LoRA npy path. With a single repo this happens to work; with multiple repo_paths it silently breaks. This is exactly the kind of bug a clearer data structure (or just non-overlapping names) prevents — rename the inner variable to lora_config_npy_path.

self.model_metadata.get(model_name) returns None when the model isn't in the dict, then the very next line dereferences model_metadata.lora_configs. The return type is annotated TritonLoraConfig but the function can also return None. Either guard the None case explicitly and raise a ClientError with a clear message, or change the contract. The annotation lies about the data — and the data is what's wrong.

issues.description: lora_task_id assignment is global across repos and not stable across reloads
issues.detail: lora_task_id starts at 1 and increments per LoRA across all repo_paths in iteration order. The TRT-LLM backend caches by task_id; if the model repo is rescanned (or LoRAs are added/removed) the task_id-to-weights mapping can shift, and a 'cached' task_id on the backend will point to different weights than the frontend believes. The data structure needs a stable, content-derived id (hash of path, or hash of weights) — or the cache invalidation contract with the backend has to be made explicit. As written, the algorithm is fighting the data.

issues.description: Per-request np.load of weights blocks the event loop and re-reads from disk on every cold LoRA
issues.detail: _create_trtllm_generate_request is invoked from an async handler but calls np.load synchronously inside the request path. For a multi-gigabyte LoRA tensor this stalls the event loop. The natural shape: load weights once at parse time (or on first use into a thread executor), keep the ndarray on the config object, and pass it by reference. Right now the data flow is request -> disk -> network on every cold path, when it should be parse -> memory -> network.

issues.description: Return type annotation on _parse_lora_configs is wrong
issues.detail: Signature says -> None | List[tuple[str, str]] but the function returns List[TritonLoraConfig] | None. Type lies. Either the reader believes the annotation and writes broken downstream code, or they ignore annotations entirely — both are bad. Fix to None | List[TritonLoraConfig].

issues.description: Stray debug print(f'backend: {backend}') in a hot configuration path
issues.detail: Inside the per-LoRA loop in _parse_lora_configs a debug print fires once per LoRA per model. Combined with the traceback prints added to the FastAPI routers and to the except Exception branch, the production logs become noisy and the actual error paths are harder to read. Use logging with levels, or drop the prints — don't ship debug breadcrumbs as features.

issues.description: traceback.print added to generic except Exception masks the real failure mode
issues.detail: The except Exception in _parse_lora_configs now does print(traceback.format_exc()); return None. So a malformed multi_lora.json silently makes the model appear LoRA-less but spams a traceback to stdout. Either this should propagate as ServerError (the file is required for the feature), or it should be a structured logger.warning with the model name and path. Right now the data structure says 'no LoRA here' and the side channel says 'something blew up' — pick one.

issues.description: List-comprehension membership check rebuilt on every validate call
issues.detail: _validate_chat_request and _validate_completion_request do `lora_name not in [lora_config.name for lora_config in metadata.lora_configs]`. That's O(n) per call plus a fresh list allocation. n is small so the cost is small — but the right data structure for membership is a set, and storing names as a set alongside the configs (or a {name: config} dict) collapses three call-sites (_validate_chat_request, _validate_completion_request, _get_lora_config) into a single hash lookup. Right now the algorithm is fighting the data shape.

issues.description: _get_model_metadata loses the explicit 'only vllm has LoRA' gate without an equivalent for non-LoRA backends
issues.detail: Previously the code only called _get_vllm_lora_names when the backend was vllm. Now _parse_lora_configs is called for every model regardless of backend, and the inner branch handles vllm vs 'else'. For an ensemble or python backend, this silently follows the 'else' path (treat as TRT-LLM, look for multi_lora.json) and skips if absent — which happens to be correct but is undocumented. Either dispatch explicitly on backend in {'vllm','tensorrtllm'} and return None otherwise, or add a comment explaining the implicit contract.

issues.description: TritonLoraConfig is a class where a small dataclass + module-level functions would do
issues.detail: The dataclass is right, but the surrounding code grew _get_lora_config on the engine, list comprehensions on every validate, and mutation on is_registered. The data wants to be a {name -> immutable config} dict plus a separate {name -> registered?} set, with two free functions: lookup(name) and mark_registered(name). That's the Pike shape — config is data, registration is state, and they don't live in the same struct. Smaller, more obvious, no race window.

issues.description: Test bifurcation by backend uses if/elif/else where dispatch table would be smaller
issues.detail: test_lora_separator_not_set, test_lora_separator_set, and test_lora_separator_set_for_lora_off_model each repeat the same if backend == 'vllm' / elif 'tensorrtllm' / else raise block. A dict {backend: setup_fn} resolved once in setUp removes nine lines of repeated dispatch and makes adding a third backend a one-line change. Small thing; the duplication is the smell.

review.summary: The feature lands a real capability but the data shape is fighting the code. The TritonLoraConfig dataclass mixes immutable config (name, path, task_id) with mutable runtime state (is_registered) and is shared across concurrent requests with no synchronization — that's a P0 race that will silently send unregistered weights to the backend or double-register them. Separately, lora_config_path is shadowed inside the parsing loop (P0), the return-type annotation lies (P1), and the synchronous np.load runs inside the async request path (P1). The right Pike-shaped fix is a {name -> immutable LoraConfig} dict on the metadata, a separate registered-set guarded by a lock, weights loaded once at parse-time, and the validate/lookup call-sites collapsed to a single hash lookup. Strip the stray debug prints and tighten the except Exception traceback before merge.
